newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Olivetti fails to please experts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Olivetti fails to please experts.

text.p: Olivetti's answers to a list of detailed questions from market regulators has left investors little wiser about the financial state of the embattled information technology group, analysts said on Wednesday.
The loss-making group, whose shares have slumped to a record low, produced answers to most of 16 detailed questions put to it by bourse watchdog Consob about the state of its finances.

"There are two big doubts about Olivetti one is over its debt and the other concerns its inventories. They have not cleared up these doubts," said a Milan-based equities analyst with a foreign investment bank who follows the company.
The company said in a statement that it could not divulge confidential information about negotiations under way on future divestments or strategic link-ups with other companies.

It also said it could not state its consolidated net debt position for the end of August 1996 until the first week of October. This was because of the need to gather "data coming from around 200 companies operating in the group."
"It's worrying that they cannot give their debt position," said an equities analyst with a Milan brokerage who asked not to be named.

"It's ridiculous that a company Olivetti's size has 200 operating companies. It means that they have big lead times and that they are not able to intervene quickly if one of those companies gets out of control."

The company said earlier this month that net debt at the end of June totalled 1.26 trillion lire ($825.1 million), but analysts believe that interest charges paid by the group suggest that it could owe much more.

"People are very perplexed by this. Olivetti should already know roughly what the position is and now we all have to wait for another three weeks before we are going to know," said a stock trader in Milan.
Analysts said Olivetti was acting within its rights in not releasing information about any talks that could lead to businesses being disposed of or to the forging of alliances with other companies.
Details of Olivetti's inventories given in its statement also failed to give industry-watchers any clues as to exactly what products are sitting unsold in Olivetti warehouses.
The company said that stocks of personal computers and of products made by its Lexikon office equipment subsidiary amounted to 105 billion and 123 billion lire, respectively.

Market commentators say they want to see a detailed breakdown of the PC models that Olivetti has in its warehouses so they can determine whether there is any obsolete equipment whose value should be written down.

"There is no point telling people what the breakdown is between Lexikon products and PCs, people want to know whether those PCs are (up-to-date) fast Pentiums of (out-of-date) 386 and 486 models," said a Milan analyst.
For some experts Olivetti's answers were of academic interest only.

"We are not that interested any more," said an equities specialist at the Milan office of a major European investment bank. "Nearly all our clients have sold Olivetti in the last few days and no one wants to get back into the stock." ($1=1527 Lire)
